trial_name: REST — Ultraprotective Ventilation with VV-ECCO2R vs Standard Care in Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure (2021)
citation: McNamee JJ, Gillies MA, Barrett NA, et al; REST Investigators. Effect of Lower Tidal Volume Ventilation Facilitated by Extracorporeal Carbon Dioxide Removal vs Standard Care Ventilation on 90-Day Mortality in Patients With Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: The REST Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2021;326(11):1013-1023.
trial_type: RCT — multicenter, pragmatic, open-label, parallel-group, superiority
one_liner: In acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, VV-ECCO2R-facilitated ultraprotective ventilation did not reduce 90-day mortality compared to standard lung-protective ventilation and was associated with significantly more serious adverse events.

pico.population: Adults with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (PaO2/FiO2 ≤150 mmHg) on invasive mechanical ventilation
pico.intervention: VV-ECCO2R (Hemolung) plus protocolised ultraprotective ventilation (target tidal volume ~3 mL/kg PBW, plateau pressure ≤25 cmH2O)
pico.comparison: Standard lung-protective ventilation without VV-ECCO2R (target tidal volume ~6 mL/kg PBW)

background.existing_knowledge: Lung-protective ventilation (lower tidal volumes) improves outcomes in acute respiratory failure, but lung injury may persist when mechanical stress (plateau/driving pressure, mechanical power) remains high.
background.knowledge_gap: Pre-REST evidence for VV-ECCO2R in ARDS/AHRF was dominated by feasibility studies and small trials, with persistent uncertainty regarding net benefit vs harm at patient-centred outcomes.
background.hypothesis: Lowering tidal volume during invasive mechanical ventilation using VV-ECCO2R (to facilitate ultraprotective ventilation) reduces 90-day mortality compared with standard lung-protective ventilation.

methods.design: Multicentre, pragmatic, open-label, randomised, parallel-group clinical trial; 51 adult ICUs (United Kingdom); 1:1 allocation; stratified by site.
methods.setting: 51 adult ICUs in the United Kingdom.

inclusion: Acute and potentially reversible cause of acute respiratory failure
Within 48 hours of onset of qualifying hypoxaemia defined by PaO2/FiO2 ≤20 kPa (≤150 mmHg) on 2 arterial blood gases separated by ≥6 hours
Randomisation occurred 8–24 hours after the second qualifying blood gas
exclusion: Invasive ventilation ≥7 days prior to randomisation
Ability to maintain tidal volume ≤3 mL/kg predicted body weight with pH ≥7.2 without VV-ECCO2R
Receipt of (or decision to commence) ECMO within 24 hours
Untreated pulmonary embolism/pleural effusion/pneumothorax as primary cause
Acute respiratory failure fully explained by left ventricular failure or fluid overload
Contraindication to limited systemic anticoagulation with heparin
Inability to obtain central venous access (IJ/femoral) or IVC filter (if femoral access)
Not expected to survive 90 days due to premorbid illness
Severe chronic respiratory disease requiring domiciliary ventilation (except sleep-disordered breathing)
Platelet count <40,000/mm3 prior to catheter insertion

methods.intervention: VV-ECCO2R (Hemolung Respiratory Assist System) plus a protocolised ultraprotective ventilatory strategy. Ventilation targets: Tidal volume target ~3 mL/kg predicted body weight; plateau pressure target ≤25 cmH2O. Duration: maximum 7 days.
methods.comparison: Standard-care ventilation without VV-ECCO2R (lung-protective ventilation; typical tidal volume target ~6 mL/kg predicted body weight, with standard plateau pressure constraints).
methods.sample_size_power: Planned sample size 1120 to detect a 9% absolute reduction in 90-day mortality (from 41% to 32%) with 90% power at the 5% significance level (two-sided). Trial stopped early after 412 participants randomised.
methods.follow_up: Primary endpoint at 90 days; key secondary outcomes to day 28.

headline_bullets: Trial stopped early for futility/feasibility after 412 patients randomised.
No significant difference in 90-day mortality: 41.5% vs 39.5% (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.83–1.33).
VV-ECCO2R group had significantly fewer ventilator-free days (mean difference −2.1 days) and a marked excess of serious adverse events (30.7% vs 8.6%).

outcomes_table.outcome: Bleeding at other site (excluding intracranial haemorrhage; any adverse event)

subgroup_table.subgroup: Prespecified subgroups (e.g., ARDS status, baseline PaO2/FiO2, plateau pressure, driving pressure, APACHE II)
subgroup_table.note: Interaction tests were not significant and confidence intervals were wide.

safety: Serious adverse events were more common in the VV-ECCO2R group (30.7% vs 8.6%).
Intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 5.0% of the VV-ECCO2R group vs 1.0% in the standard care group.
Non-intracranial bleeding occurred in 8.4% of the VV-ECCO2R group vs 1.4% in the standard care group.

domains.notes: Central randomisation with stratification by site. Baseline balance was good across key prognostic factors (e.g., median PaO2/FiO2 118.1 vs 115.5 mmHg; APACHE II 19 vs 20).

Unblinded delivery is unavoidable for VV-ECCO2R. Mortality is objective, but ventilator-free days and weaning-related endpoints are vulnerable to differences in sedation, ventilator mode, and clinician behaviour.
Primary analysis included 405/412 randomised (200 vs 205), indicating low missingness for the primary endpoint.
186/202 (92.1%) allocated to VV-ECCO2R received it. 1 patient in the control group received non-protocol VV-ECCO2R for 2 days (minimal crossover).
Good balance across key prognostic factors.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate. Randomisation and baseline balance support a credible estimate for mortality, but early stopping and unblinded care with systematic differences in sedation/ventilation mode limit interpretability of weaning-related secondary outcomes.

domains.notes: Adults with moderate-to-severe acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure treated in general UK ICUs; baseline severity (median PaO2/FiO2 ~116–118 mmHg; APACHE II ~19–20; SOFA ~10) is typical of patients considered for escalated ventilatory strategies.

VV-ECCO2R requires specialised equipment, cannulation skills, and anticoagulation management; transferability is limited to centres with established extracorporeal capability. In resource-limited settings, the risk–resource trade-off is likely even less favourable.

external_validity.verdict: Moderate. The clinical phenotype is common, but the intervention is highly specialised and the observed harm burden makes routine extrapolation beyond controlled settings and experienced centres difficult to justify.

strengths: Pragmatic, multicentre design across 51 ICUs enhances real-world relevance.
Objective primary endpoint (90-day all-cause mortality) with low missingness reduces susceptibility to ascertainment bias.
Demonstrated physiologic separation in ventilation variables (lower tidal volume, plateau and driving pressure) verifies that the biological “lever” was at least partially pulled.
Detailed reporting of ventilation parameters and adverse events enables granular assessment of efficacy–harm trade-offs.
limitations: Stopped early for futility/feasibility: substantial loss of statistical power for the prespecified mortality effect; mortality CI remains wide.
Open-label management and systematic differences in controlled ventilation/neuromuscular blockade likely confound ventilator-free days.
Ultraprotective “dose” may have been insufficient: delivered tidal volumes were ~4–4.5 mL/kg PBW rather than the ~3 mL/kg PBW target, and VV-ECCO2R duration averaged 4 days.
Safety signal: substantial bleeding and device-related harms materially constrain benefit–risk acceptability.

critical_appraisal.summary: A well-conducted but early-stopped trial showing no mortality benefit and significant harm from VV-ECCO2R-facilitated ultraprotective ventilation, with moderate internal and external validity.
strengths: Objective primary endpoint with low missingness
Clear physiologic separation of the intervention
weaknesses: Inability to achieve the target ultraprotective tidal volume

sections.authors_conclusion: In a broad UK ICU population with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure, VV-ECCO2R-facilitated ultraprotective ventilation did not reduce 90-day mortality and increased serious adverse events; routine use cannot be justified on these data.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: This trial does not support the routine use of VV-ECCO2R to facilitate ultraprotective ventilation in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. The intervention did not improve survival and caused significant harm.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adults with moderate-to-severe acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (PaO2/FiO2 ≤150 mmHg) on invasive mechanical ventilation.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: That all extracorporeal support strategies are harmful. This trial specifically tested low-flow VV-ECCO2R for ultraprotective ventilation, not full ECMO for refractory hypoxemia.
implementation_caveats: The significant increase in serious adverse events, particularly intracranial haemorrhage, is a major deterrent to use.
The reduction in ventilator-free days may be a direct consequence of the deeper sedation required to deliver the intervention.

controversies.notes: The prespecified mortality effect size was ambitious; stopping at 412 randomised patients left wide uncertainty around clinically meaningful benefit or harm.

The VV-ECCO2R group received more controlled ventilation and neuromuscular blockade early, creating a credible pathway for delayed weaning/extubation that is not necessarily reflective of worse lung recovery.
Serious adverse events were common in VV-ECCO2R (30.7% vs 8.6%), including intracranial haemorrhage (5.0% vs 1.0%), raising the bar for any future efficacy signal.

Earlier randomised work (e.g., Xtravent) established feasibility but not patient-centred benefit; REST provides the clearest signal that feasibility does not translate into mortality benefit and that harms are non-trivial.

context_related_trials.relation: Earlier randomised work establishing feasibility of ECCO2R-facilitated ultraprotective ventilation but not patient-centred benefit.

unresolved_questions: Is there a specific subgroup (e.g., very high VILI risk, severe hypercapnia) that might benefit from VV-ECCO2R?
Can safer devices or anticoagulation strategies mitigate the bleeding risk to make the risk-benefit profile more favourable?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: VV-ECCO2R for ultraprotective ventilation in AHRF does not improve survival and causes significant bleeding; do not use outside of trials.
